articles.title: Brain area discovered that may be critical for viable pregnancies
articles.summary: A newly discovered part of the brain is essential for successful embryo implantation in mice. It may help to explain why some pregnancies and IVF attempts fail
articles.content:
A newly discovered part of the brain is essential for successful embryo implantation in mice. It may help to explain why some pregnancies and IVF attempts fail

Neurons that comprise fewer than 0.001 per cent of all brain cells may be crucial for maintaining a pregnancy Yiu Yu Hoi/Getty Images

A tiny set of neurons deep inside the brain is fundamental to viable pregnancies in mice. These neurons are also present in human female brains and could provide clues about unexplained recurrent miscarriages and IVF difficulties.

Nirao Shah at Stanford University, California, and his colleagues discovered the neurons while looking for gene expression changes in different parts of the female mouse brain during pregnancy. They observed a small population of neurons that completely transformed.

The levels of gene expression in these neurons changed over 30-fold when mice became pregnant for the first time, converting them to a new class of neurons that functioned in a completely different way by mid-gestation. “This cell type is exclusive to pregnancy,” the researchers write.

Advertisement

The previously unknown set of neurons is in an area deep in the centre of the brain called the preoptic hypothalamus, which is also involved in sexual and parental behaviours. The neurons have receptors for pregnancy-related hormones like progesterone, which may be responsible for switching the neurons on after the initial fertilisation of an egg.

Once activated, these neurons appear to coordinate the implantation of the embryo in the uterus and maintain the ongoing pregnancy. When Shah’s team created female mice without this special type of neuron, the mice were able to mate and become pregnant, but their pregnancies all ended at an early stage. This was because their embryos couldn’t implant in the lining of the uterus.

“Certainly, the fact that when you get rid of these neurons, you lose these pregnancies, is really suggestive,” says Jennifer O’Chan at the Icahn School of Medicine at Mount Sinai, New York.

These neurons comprise fewer than 0.001 per cent of all brain cells, making it remarkable that their selective elimination completely blocks the ability to establish viable pregnancies, write Shah and his colleagues.

However, further research will be required to investigate how these neurons actually do this, says O’Chan. “They’ve shown that these neurons change robustly during pregnancy, but then how are they actually communicating with the uterus? Is it hormonal? Are they secreting some kind of factor? If they could identify that, I would be very convinced.”

It would also be interesting to study whether these neurons are permanently changed by pregnancy or eventually return to their original state, says O’Chan, since her own research has found that pregnancy induces long-lasting changes in the brain.

Free newsletter Sign up to Health Check Sign up to newsletter

Shah’s team also analysed an existing atlas of gene expression in the human brain and found that women have the same special set of neurons in their preoptic hypothalamus, hinting these neurons may play a similar role in human pregnancies. “You can’t do these types of experiments in humans, so we have to extrapolate here, but mouse and human brains do tend to be fairly well-conserved,” says O’Chan.

Just over half of miscarriages are known to be caused by genetic errors in the embryo, but the rest can’t be explained. For example, some people undergoing IVF have multiple embryos that appear genetically healthy, but none seem to implant once they are inserted in the uterus, for reasons that are unclear. Some who conceive naturally also have recurrent early pregnancy losses for no detectable reason.

According to Shah and his colleagues, these fertility challenges may relate to the neurons they discovered, potentially paving the way for new treatments. “We speculate that a subset of such events reflects failure of particular neural circuits to recognize, monitor, or adapt to gestation,” they write.

“If, for example, you found that these neurons were releasing a fundamental signalling molecule that was important for implantation, you might be able to turn that into a therapeutic for people with fertility issues,” says O’Chan.
articles.reasoning: The discovery of a brain area critical for embryo implantation in mice, also present in humans, offers significant insights into unexplained miscarriages and IVF failures, potentially leading to new fertility treatments. This represents a meaningful scientific breakthrough with broad implications for reproductive health.
articles.personality_title: New brain cells found that may help explain pregnancy success
articles.personality_presentation:
**Context** – Scientists have been trying to understand why some pregnancies end early or why some IVF treatments do not work. Many early pregnancy losses happen without a clear reason.

**What happened** – Researchers at Stanford University discovered a tiny group of brain cells in female mice that change a lot during pregnancy. These cells, found deep in a brain area called the preoptic hypothalamus, help embryos attach to the uterus and keep the pregnancy going. When these cells were removed in mice, pregnancies failed early because embryos could not implant. The same type of cells also exist in humans.

**Impact** – This discovery is important because it shows that a very small number of brain cells can control pregnancy success. It helps explain some cases of miscarriage and IVF failure that doctors could not previously understand. Knowing about these brain cells could lead to new ways to treat fertility problems.

**What's next step** – Scientists want to learn exactly how these brain cells help the embryo attach to the uterus. They will study whether the cells send signals or hormones to the uterus. Researchers also want to find out if pregnancy changes these cells permanently. This knowledge could help develop new fertility treatments.

**One-sentence takeaway** – A tiny group of brain cells may be key to successful pregnancy by helping embryos implant, offering new hope for understanding and treating fertility issues.
articles.personality_title_fr: De nouvelles cellules cérébrales découvertes qui pourraient expliquer le succès de la grossesse
articles.personality_presentation_fr:
**Contexte** – Les scientifiques cherchent à comprendre pourquoi certaines grossesses s'arrêtent tôt ou pourquoi certains traitements de FIV échouent. Beaucoup de pertes de grossesse précoces restent inexpliquées.

**Ce qui s’est passé** – Des chercheurs de l’Université Stanford ont découvert un petit groupe de cellules cérébrales chez la souris femelle qui changent beaucoup pendant la grossesse. Ces cellules, situées dans une zone profonde du cerveau appelée hypothalamus préoptique, aident l’embryon à s’attacher à l’utérus et à maintenir la grossesse. Quand ces cellules ont été retirées chez la souris, les grossesses ont échoué car l’embryon ne pouvait pas s’implanter. Ce type de cellules existe aussi chez l’humain.

**Impact** – Cette découverte est importante car elle montre qu’un très petit nombre de cellules cérébrales peut contrôler le succès de la grossesse. Cela aide à expliquer certains cas de fausses couches et d’échecs de FIV jusque-là incompris. Connaître ces cellules pourrait permettre de nouveaux traitements pour les problèmes de fertilité.

**Prochaine étape** – Les scientifiques veulent comprendre comment ces cellules aident l’embryon à s’implanter. Ils étudieront si elles envoient des signaux ou des hormones à l’utérus. Ils veulent aussi savoir si la grossesse change ces cellules de façon permanente. Ces recherches pourraient conduire à de nouveaux traitements de fertilité.

**Phrase clé** – Un petit groupe de cellules cérébrales pourrait être essentiel à la réussite de la grossesse en aidant l’embryon à s’implanter, ouvrant de nouvelles pistes pour comprendre et traiter les problèmes de fertilité.
articles.personality_title_es: Nuevas células cerebrales descubiertas que podrían explicar el éxito del embarazo
articles.personality_presentation_es:
**Contexto** – Los científicos buscan entender por qué algunos embarazos terminan temprano o por qué algunos tratamientos de fertilización in vitro (FIV) no funcionan. Muchas pérdidas tempranas del embarazo no tienen una causa clara.

**Qué ocurrió** – Investigadores de la Universidad de Stanford descubrieron un pequeño grupo de células cerebrales en ratonas que cambian mucho durante el embarazo. Estas células, ubicadas en una zona profunda del cerebro llamada hipotálamo preóptico, ayudan al embrión a implantarse en el útero y mantener el embarazo. Cuando estas células fueron eliminadas en ratonas, los embarazos fallaron porque el embrión no pudo implantarse. El mismo tipo de células también existe en humanos.

**Impacto** – Este descubrimiento es importante porque muestra que un número muy pequeño de células cerebrales puede controlar el éxito del embarazo. Ayuda a explicar algunos casos de aborto espontáneo y fallos en la FIV que antes no se entendían. Conocer estas células podría llevar a nuevos tratamientos para problemas de fertilidad.

articles.title: Global life expectancy bounces back to near pre-pandemic levels, WHO says
articles.summary: People around the world are living longer again, with global life expectancy almost fully recovered from the disruption of the COVID-19 pandemic, the World Health Organization (WHO) said on Friday.
articles.content:
According to the UN health agency’s latest Global Health Estimates, life expectancy reached 73.3 years in 2023, just shy of the 73.4 years recorded in 2019.

Tweet URL

“Living longer is one of the great achievements of public health,” said Dr. Alain Labrique, Director of WHO’s Department of Data, Digital Health, Analytics and AI.

The estimates, which cover trends in death and disability worldwide by region and by country from 2000 to 2023, draw on various sources including national vital registration data and estimates from WHO technical programmes alongside UN partner organizations.

Healthy life expectancy – the years people live in good health – has recovered more slowly, reaching 62.8 years in 2023, still 0.4 years below its 2019 level.

“The next challenge is to ensure that those additional years are lived in good health, while health systems are equipped to respond to the changing needs of populations,” Dr. Labrique said.

Milestone for low-income countries

The estimates also point to a long-term shift in what people die from.

In 2023, for the first time, communicable diseases – one that spreads from one person or animal to another, or from a surface to a person – accounted for less than half of all deaths in low-income countries, a further step in what WHO calls the “global epidemiological transition”.

Worldwide, noncommunicable diseases (NCDs) caused 74 per cent of deaths in 2023, up from 58 per cent in 2000, and eight of the world’s 10 leading causes of death were NCDs.

Cardiovascular diseases remain the leading cause of death and disease burden. Ischaemic heart disease alone caused approximately 9.5 million deaths in 2023 and the loss of 210 million years of healthy life.

Many parts of the world have made substantial progress in reducing that burden since 2000, though individual risk increased in Western Pacific and Southeast Asia regions, highlighting persistent inequalities.

WHO/Yoshi Shimizu

Rising burden of dementia

Other chronic conditions are becoming more prominent. Dementia rose from the 19th leading cause of death globally in 2000 to the fifth in 2023, with deaths from the condition tripling over the period.

The risk of dying from diabetes has also risen substantially since 2000, particularly in South-East Asia.

Between 2019 and 2023, the global age-standardised rate of “healthy life” lost rose by about 20 per cent for depressive disorders and nearly 45 per cent for anxiety disorders.

For drug use disorders, the Americas recorded the largest increases in risk of death and healthy life lost between 2000 and 2023, while the Western Pacific saw substantial declines.

Diagnosis points to cure

“The value of these estimates is not only in the numbers themselves,” Dr. Labrique said. “By showing how causes of death and disease burden are changing over time and across populations, they give countries evidence to help shape health policies and priorities.”
articles.source: UN News - Global perspective Human stories

articles.title: First week of life seems crucial for future allergy and eczema risk
articles.summary: The mainstream view is that there are no particularly critical phases in the development of the immune system, but a study of hundreds of infants suggests otherwise
articles.content:
The mainstream view is that there are no particularly critical phases in the development of the immune system, but a study of hundreds of infants suggests otherwise

The immune reactions we experience in the first week of life may have a lasting impact Agung Putu Surya Purna Kristyaw/Getty Images

Babies who have a strong immune reaction in the first week of life seem to have triple the risk of developing an allergy or eczema by age 1, compared with those who don’t. But the long-term impact of this early immune response, now defined for the first time, seems to be modulated by the microbiome and how babies are fed.

“If you ask 100 immunologists, they would say that immune development begins at birth and continuously develops over time, without discrete phases,” says Petter Brodin at Imperial College London.

But at a talk at an immune conference in London earlier this month, Brodin challenged this idea. He revealed that he and his colleagues have found that if a baby has a strong immune response in the first week of life, this seems to have an oversized impact on how the infant’s immune system subsequently develops. “That’s a novel concept,” he said during the talk.

Advertisement

In ongoing research, Brodin and his colleagues have been studying nearly 600 infants in Sweden, collecting and analysing blood and stool samples from the infants throughout their first year of life. The analysis revealed that about half the babies had what the researchers termed a strong “seeding” immune reaction during the first week of life, marked by high levels of inflammatory molecules such as interferon gamma, which activates immune cells. The remaining infants had lower levels of these inflammatory molecules during the first week, which the team called a weak seeding reaction.

Further analysis revealed that babies with a strong seeding reaction had substantially more Bacteroides bacteria in their gut than those who had a weak reaction. “A high abundance of Bacteroides bacteria seems to drive seeding reactions to be very strong,” says Brodin – although it is also possible that the variation in levels of the bacteria actually resulted from differences in the severity of the seeding reaction. Babies can pick up these bacteria via interactions with their mother and family members, he says.

The researchers think the effects of the seeding reaction last for only about a week at the beginning of life because that is when the gut is especially leaky, enabling bacteria like Bacteroides to enter the bloodstream and activate immune cells. “Healthy infants are born with a leaky gut that closes up after about a week,” says Brodin.

Make me well: How to outsmart the wellness industry See Chris and Xand van Tulleken at New Scientist Live 2026 Find out more

But the seeding reaction may have lasting effects: by sifting through the infants’ medical records, the researchers found that 39 per cent of those with a strong seeding reaction developed either eczema or a food allergy by age 1. In contrast, just 12 per cent of infants with a weak seeding reaction developed at least one of these conditions, which are caused by excessive inflammation. “What we ideally want is a weak seeding reaction,” says Brodin.

Further analysis revealed that the infants with a strong reaction then followed one of three immune trajectories linked to two main factors: whether they were primarily fed breast or formula milk, and the abundance of bifidobacteria in their gut.

For instance, 50 per cent of babies who had a strong seeding reaction and were breastfed – but had low levels of bifidobacteria – developed eczema or food allergies. Breastfed infants who had a strong seeding reaction and had high bifidobacteria levels were less likely to develop eczema or food allergies, with 25 per cent of them doing so.

The researchers also found that 33 per cent of infants who had a strong seeding reaction and were fed formula milk developed eczema or an allergy by age 1. In the work presented at the conference, the team didn’t give details of bifidobacteria levels in the guts of these formula-fed babies.

Brodin says the bifidobacteria may be important because they break down certain sugars in breast milk, known as human milk oligosaccharides (HMOs), to produce anti-inflammatory molecules called short-chain fatty acids. In turn, these can prevent the immune system from overreacting, he says. The researchers plan to explore why exactly the other links may have emerged in future research, says Brodin.

“This is a really important piece of work. Only a few studies have looked at immune development during the first week after birth,” says Lucy Crouch at the University of Birmingham in the UK. The research could reveal ways to develop personalised medicine for infants, she says.

For instance, you could imagine measuring whether a baby has a strong or weak seeding reaction, then, depending on whether they are breastfed or not and their levels of bifidobacteria, you could give them a probiotic that boosts these microbes to cut their allergy or eczema risk, she says.

But further research is needed to establish whether the seeding reaction has effects beyond the first year, says Crouch. Studies should also explore whether the links made in the study really are causal, she says, which could be done by tracking how immune cells within gut organoids – clumps of lab-grown cells that are used to mimic the intestines – react to bacteria in the presence or absence of HMOs.

“The reported differences in allergy and eczema risk are striking, but they show associations rather than demonstrating that particular microbes or immune responses directly cause the later outcomes,” says Lindsay Hall, also at the University of Birmingham.

For now, parents shouldn’t alter how they feed or interact with their infants based on the results. “It is much too early to suggest that the findings should change advice to parents,” says Hall.
articles.reasoning: The article reports a significant scientific discovery about the early immune system development in infants and its impact on allergy and eczema risk, which could lead to personalized medicine and preventive strategies benefiting many children globally. The study is well-detailed, involves a large sample size, and highlights potential interventions through microbiome modulation, making it a meaningful advancement in health research.
articles.personality_title: Early immune response in newborns linked to allergy risk by age one
articles.personality_presentation:
**Context** – Scientists have generally believed that the immune system develops steadily after birth without any special critical periods. Allergies and eczema are common problems in babies, but how early immune reactions affect these conditions was unclear.

**What happened** – Researchers studied nearly 600 infants in Sweden and found that babies who showed a strong immune reaction in their first week of life were three times more likely to develop allergies or eczema by age one. This strong reaction involved high levels of inflammatory molecules and more Bacteroides bacteria in the gut. The study also showed that breastfed babies with higher levels of another type of bacteria, bifidobacteria, had a lower risk of developing these conditions.

**Impact** – This discovery suggests the first week of life is a crucial period when the immune system’s reaction can shape future allergy and eczema risk. It also shows that gut bacteria and feeding methods, like breastfeeding, play important roles. Understanding this could help doctors create personalized treatments to reduce allergies by supporting healthy gut bacteria early on.

**What's next step** – Scientists want to study how these immune reactions affect children beyond their first year and test if giving probiotics to boost helpful bacteria can prevent allergies. They also plan to use lab-grown gut cells to better understand how bacteria and breast milk sugars influence the immune system.

**One-sentence takeaway** – A baby’s immune reaction in the first week, influenced by gut bacteria and feeding, may predict their chance of allergies or eczema by age one, opening new paths for early prevention.
articles.personality_title_fr: La réponse immunitaire précoce des nouveau-nés liée au risque d’allergies avant un an
articles.personality_presentation_fr:
**Contexte** – Les scientifiques pensaient généralement que le système immunitaire se développe progressivement après la naissance, sans périodes critiques particulières. Les allergies et l’eczéma sont fréquents chez les bébés, mais on ne savait pas comment les réactions immunitaires précoces influençaient ces problèmes.

**Ce qui s’est passé** – Des chercheurs suédois ont étudié près de 600 nourrissons et ont découvert que ceux ayant une forte réaction immunitaire dans leur première semaine de vie avaient trois fois plus de risques de développer des allergies ou de l’eczéma avant l’âge d’un an. Cette forte réaction impliquait des niveaux élevés de molécules inflammatoires et plus de bactéries Bacteroides dans l’intestin. L’étude a aussi montré que les bébés allaités avec plus de bifidobactéries avaient un risque plus faible.

**Impact** – Cette découverte suggère que la première semaine de vie est une période clé où la réaction immunitaire peut influencer le risque futur d’allergies et d’eczéma. Elle montre aussi que les bactéries intestinales et l’allaitement jouent un rôle important. Cela pourrait aider les médecins à créer des traitements personnalisés pour réduire les allergies en soutenant les bonnes bactéries.

**Prochaine étape** – Les scientifiques veulent étudier les effets de ces réactions immunitaires au-delà de la première année et tester si des probiotiques peuvent prévenir les allergies. Ils prévoient aussi d’utiliser des cellules intestinales cultivées en laboratoire pour mieux comprendre l’influence des bactéries et des sucres du lait maternel.

**Résumé en une phrase** – La réaction immunitaire d’un bébé dans la première semaine, influencée par les bactéries intestinales et l’alimentation, peut prédire son risque d’allergies ou d’eczéma avant un an, ouvrant la voie à une prévention précoce.
articles.personality_title_es: La respuesta inmunitaria temprana en recién nacidos vinculada al riesgo de alergias antes del año
articles.personality_presentation_es:
**Contexto** – Los científicos creían que el sistema inmunitario se desarrolla de forma continua tras el nacimiento, sin fases críticas especiales. Las alergias y el eczema son comunes en bebés, pero no se sabía cómo las reacciones inmunitarias tempranas influían en estos problemas.

**Qué pasó** – Investigadores en Suecia estudiaron a casi 600 bebés y encontraron que aquellos con una fuerte reacción inmunitaria en la primera semana de vida tenían tres veces más riesgo de desarrollar alergias o eczema antes del año. Esta reacción fuerte incluía altos niveles de moléculas inflamatorias y más bacterias Bacteroides en el intestino. El estudio también mostró que los bebés amamantados con más bifidobacterias tenían menos riesgo.

**Impacto** – Este hallazgo indica que la primera semana de vida es un período clave donde la reacción inmunitaria puede afectar el riesgo futuro de alergias y eczema. También muestra que las bacterias intestinales y la alimentación, como la lactancia, son importantes. Esto podría ayudar a crear tratamientos personalizados para reducir alergias apoyando las bacterias buenas.

**Próximo paso** – Los científicos quieren estudiar los efectos de estas reacciones más allá del primer año y probar si los probióticos pueden prevenir alergias. También planean usar células intestinales cultivadas en laboratorio para entender mejor cómo las bacterias y los azúcares de la leche materna afectan al sistema inmunitario.

**Resumen en una frase** – La reacción inmunitaria de un bebé en la primera semana, influida por bacterias intestinales y alimentación, puede predecir su riesgo de alergias o eczema antes del año, abriendo caminos para la prevención temprana.
